e.t: This is a proper name, rendered “Abdōn” or “Avthon,” used to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Judges and once in 2 Chronicles. The available references preserve the name, but no surrounding verse text is provided here, so the broader significance of each occurrence cannot be stated from the name alone. Its basic meaning is the personal name Abdōn, also rendered Avthon.

This adjective describes someone or something that does not die—something “undying” or “immortal.” It points to enduring life rather than ordinary mortal existence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs five times, all in the Deuterocanonical writings. Its basic meaning remains consistent across those uses, while the surrounding sentence determines whether it describes a person, a quality, or something viewed as lasting beyond death.

Ailōm, also rendered Elom, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, across three verses in Joshua and Judges. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise referent therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the specific biblical context.

Akatan is a personal name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek text, in Ezra 8:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be explained further from this word alone. Its basic meaning, therefore, is simply the proper name Akatan.

The word is the proper name “Amathar.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Joshua 19:13. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s particular referent cannot be identified more precisely from this lexical entry alone. The entry preserves only the name itself, not an extended definition or description.

Ana is a proper name used for a person or persons in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea; its basic function is to identify someone by name. This name occurs 355 times in the LXX corpus, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Song of Songs. The exact person identified by Ana depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: not yet come to man's estate; beardless
d: not yet come to man's estate; beardless

e.t: This adjective describes someone who has not yet reached manhood, or who is still beardless. It points to an immature male in terms of age or physical development, rather than expressing a moral judgment. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:13. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how the description functions there, but its basic meaning is a male who has not yet come to man’s estate.

This verb means “write against”: it describes putting something into writing in opposition or response to what has already been written. As a verb, it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees. The precise force of the action in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

“Hatefully” describes an action, attitude, or manner carried out with hatred or strong hostility. As an adverb, it tells how someone speaks, treats another person, or acts, rather than naming the person or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 19:15 and 3 Maccabees 5:3. Without the surrounding verse text, its exact force in either passage cannot be explained further, but its basic sense is clear: something is done in a hateful, hostile way.

This Greek LXX verb means “laid away” or “reserved,” describing something set aside or kept for a later purpose. It can refer to something placed in readiness rather than used immediately. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on the sentence where it occurs. It is found in Genesis, Job, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees.

This adjective describes something that remains after other things have been removed, used, or accounted for—what is left over or left behind. It can refer to a remaining portion, space, or part rather than to something newly added. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, all in Ezekiel, especially in the detailed descriptions of the temple and its surrounding areas. Its precise reference depends on the noun or place being described in each sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means to “broil” or “cook.” It describes preparing food by heating it, and it functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 36:22. The reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific action in that passage. Its basic meaning remains the act of cooking, especially by broiling.

This verb means “coin money”—to produce or mint money. It describes the act of making coins rather than simply possessing, counting, or spending them. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 6:29. Because no verse text is included here, the word’s precise force in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context; its basic lexical sense remains the making of money. The word is an action word, focusing attention on the work of producing coined currency.

This adjective describes someone who is focused chiefly on self and personal interests. It portrays a person whose outlook is self-centered rather than humble or concerned with others. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times: twice in Genesis and once in Proverbs. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a self-focused attitude or character.

Baalia, also rendered Vaalia, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:6. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its name meaning. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

“Bēthleem; Vithleem” is a proper name for the place known in English as Bethlehem. It identifies a town in the Old Testament writings represented by the Greek Septuagint. This name occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, Judges, 1 Samuel, Jeremiah, and Micah. Because it is a place name rather than a descriptive term, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader which town is being mentioned.

This Greek LXX noun means “intent”: what someone has in mind or means to accomplish. It describes a deliberate aim rather than an accidental result, so it can identify the direction behind a decision, plan, or action. The word occurs 162 times in the Greek LXX, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used broadly for purposes or intentions. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a proper name, meaning “Gazouba; Gazuva.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in 1 Kings and twice in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verse text would be needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “spawn” or “product”: something brought forth or produced. It can refer to living offspring or to the yield produced by land and labor, depending on the sentence. The word appears 72 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic idea applies broadly to what comes from a source. Its precise sense in any verse depends on what is being produced there.

Dabirōn is a proper name, also given as “Thaviron.” It is not presented as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a specific name in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX text, at Joshua 19:20. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular role there cannot be explained further; its clear lexical sense is the name itself.

Daemia, also rendered Thaemia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named individual or designation in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Nehemiah 7:7. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, but the available lexical information supports treating it as a name, not translating it as an ordinary descriptive term.

gl: greet with the right hand; welcome
d: greet with the right hand; welcome

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “greet with the right hand” or “welcome.” It describes an action of receiving or greeting someone, with the right hand serving as the visible expression of welcome. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 4:34. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its wider context, which are needed to explain the particular action described there.

δημιουργέω means to practise a trade or do work. It is a verb describing purposeful activity carried out through an occupation or practical labor, rather than simply naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains active work or practicing a craft.

This word means “seventy,” the number that comes after sixty-nine and before seventy-one. It functions as an indeclinable number, so it identifies a quantity without changing its form. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it is used 97 times, referring to counted people, objects, or amounts. Its basic meaning remains numerical; the surrounding verse determines what is being counted and whether the number has any additional significance in that passage.

Edrain, also rendered Ethren, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament’s wording, though the available information does not specify which in every occurrence. The name appears eight times across Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua, spanning Israel’s wilderness journey and the later land records. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning is the name “Edrain” or “Ethren.”

This adjective describes something “out of law,” “lawless,” or “horrible.” It identifies conduct or a thing as outside what is lawful and therefore morally disturbing or dreadful. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, in 4 Maccabees 5:14. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the precise force of the description in that sentence must be determined from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means “vanish”: to disappear or pass out of sight. It describes an action rather than a person or object, telling what someone or something does. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical writings represented here, with three occurrences in Old Testament books and one in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains disappearance.

This Greek LXX verb means “scare away”: to frighten someone or something so that it retreats or goes off. It describes an active act of driving away through fear, rather than merely feeling afraid. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 17:9. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the removal of someone or something by frightening it.

Elymais, also rendered Elimes, is a proper name for a place or region. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a geographical name preserved in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus: once in Daniel 8:2 and once in 1 Maccabees 6:1. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the place-name Elymais.

This Greek LXX noun means “mockery”—words or actions that ridicule, scorn, or make a person or thing seem foolish. It names an expression of derision rather than a neutral statement. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either passage depends on the context in which the mockery appears.

This Greek LXX verb means “let drop into”: it describes allowing something to fall or be lowered into a place. As a verb, it expresses an action or permission rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Ezekiel 21:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of letting something drop into a specified place.

This adverb means “this place” or “back here,” directing attention to a location. It points to where someone or something is, or indicates movement or return to a place understood from the sentence. Its meaning is spatial and usually depends on the surrounding words to identify exactly which place is intended. The word occurs 75 times in this Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is a recurring way to point readers or hearers toward a particular location.

This Greek LXX verb means to “slip out”—to get away or leave quietly. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish Scripture represented here, once in Job and once in Sirach. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic idea remains a quiet or unnoticed departure. The word is therefore best understood as an action of escaping, leaving, or getting free without drawing attention.

This verb describes breathing hard—panting while engaged in strenuous work. It refers to the physical act of laboring with force or exertion, not to a broad feeling or abstract idea. Its basic meaning is “breathe hard; pant in working.” In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:11. The word therefore presents a vivid physical picture of someone breathing heavily during demanding labor.

This verb means to trouble— to cause difficulty, disturbance, or distress. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:24. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of troubling. This Greek LXX noun means “labour” or “work”: effort or activity undertaken to accomplish something. It names the work itself rather than functioning as a verb for doing it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the precise shade of meaning in that occurrence must be read from its context; the basic sense remains purposeful labour or work.

This noun refers to a day-labourer or hired servant: someone engaged to work for pay. It describes a worker by the kind of service he provides, rather than naming a permanent status or personal identity. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Isaiah 38:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person hired to perform labour.

This adjective describes someone or something that is well-disposed or favourable. It expresses a positive attitude or readiness toward another person, group, or matter, rather than hostility or opposition. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 8:8. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains one of goodwill, favor, or a favorable disposition.

This noun means “command”—an authoritative direction or order given to someone. It refers to what a person is instructed to do, rather than to the act of commanding itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 9:31. The surrounding verse text is not available, so the precise force of the word in that passage must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains a command or directive.

This noun means “that which gives a relish”—something that adds relish to another thing. It refers to a substance or item valued for the taste it contributes, rather than describing an action or a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 9 verses. Its precise application depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains something that makes food or another offering more pleasing in taste.

Tharthak is a proper name, referring to a specific figure or deity named in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general description or action-word, so its basic meaning is its identifying name rather than a broader concept. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 17:31. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the name’s precise role in that passage.

Thoada, also known as Thoatha, is a personal name rather than a descriptive word. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles chapter 4. The available rendering gives the name as “Thoada,” while the lexical definition also preserves “Thoatha” as an associated form. Because it is a proper name, its main function is to identify a person, not to express an action, quality, or idea.

“Iabnē; Iavni” is a proper name, referring to a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 26:6. The available lexical information preserves the name in these forms but does not provide enough context to describe the named entity more specifically. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Iaiēl, also rendered Iil, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezra 10:26. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is its role as an identifying designation; the surrounding verse is needed to know which person is intended and how that person fits the passage. The name belongs to the LXX wording and should not be treated as a common noun or as a general theological term.

Iarimoth is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered “Iarimōth; Iarimoth,” preserving the name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing in 1 Chronicles and Ezra. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the specific individuals associated with the name cannot be identified from this lexical entry alone.

This noun refers to an idol or an amulet—a physical object associated with religious devotion or protection. Its basic meaning identifies the object itself, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:40. The reference identifies where the word appears, but the precise force of the term in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Isathi is a personal name, identifying someone rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:11. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its reference to that individual; the available information does not provide a separate descriptive definition or etymology. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This Greek LXX verb means “undermine”: to weaken or damage the support of something so that it becomes less stable or able to stand. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, and can refer to damaging structures or foundations in a literal sense. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “run down,” describing movement downward or the act of pursuing and overtaking someone. It presents an action rather than a person or thing. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across passages from Leviticus through 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains moving down toward someone or something, often with the sense of pressing after it.

This noun means a herald: a person appointed to publicly announce a message or proclamation. It describes someone who speaks or declares information on behalf of an authority, rather than merely communicating a private thought. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a public messenger who makes an announcement known.

This Greek LXX noun means “sea-crow,” referring to a sea-associated creature or bird. It is a specific name rather than a description of an action, emotion, or moral quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Jeremiah and once in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This verb means “drink hard; get drunk,” describing heavy drinking that leads to intoxication. It functions as an action word, focusing on what people do rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:15. The exact force of the word in that verse is best understood alongside the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is drinking heavily or becoming drunk.

This noun means “spoil” or “booty”—property taken from an enemy or gained in war. It refers to material goods acquired through victory, rather than to the act of taking them. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means to beg or pray; it describes making an appeal or request. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Job 17:2. That single occurrence marks its limited attested range in this corpus, while its definition points to an action of pleading rather than a name, object, or quality. Its precise force in Job 17:2 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Maanaim, also rendered Maanem, is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. The name identifies a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in Joshua 13:30 and 1 Chronicles 6:65. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the place’s history or significance; those details belong to the passages where it appears.

Mathania is a proper name, referring to a person named Mathania rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in seven verses: four in Ezra and three in Nehemiah. The available lexical definition identifies the name simply as “Mathania.” Its precise identity and role in any particular passage depend on the surrounding verse and its wider context.

Marōdachbaladan, also rendered Marothakhvalathan, is a proper name for a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 20:12. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily its identification of that individual; the name itself does not provide a general instruction or spiritual concept apart from the passage in which the person is mentioned.

This noun means “righteousness” or “justice”: what is upright, fair, and right. It names a quality rather than an action, describing moral rightness or just dealing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 70:21, and its precise force there belongs to that verse’s surrounding context. The word is rendered “righteousness” in that occurrence, confirming its central sense without adding another meaning.

“Afterward” refers to something that happens later, following an earlier action or event. As an adverb, it tells when something takes place rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, this word occurs twice, in Esther 3:13 and 3 Maccabees 3:24. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it points the reader forward in time to what follows. The surrounding verse determines which earlier event it comes after, but the word itself expresses sequence—something happening afterward.

This adverb means “from no place,” describing something as coming from nowhere or from no identifiable location. It answers the question of where something comes from, rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a denial of any place of origin.

Mōphath, also rendered Mofath, is a proper name. As a name, it identifies a particular person, place, or other named entity rather than expressing a general action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:21. The available information identifies the name and its location but does not provide enough surrounding text to determine exactly whom or what it names there.

This verb means “fast.” It describes the action of fasting, functioning as a verb rather than as a name for a fast. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 25 times across 22 verses, showing that it is a recurring action word. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains clear: to fast.

Ozriel, also rendered Ozril, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 12:7. Since it is a proper name, its main function is to identify a particular person in the biblical record. The name itself does not provide enough information here to explain that person's character, role, or significance; those details require the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “disdain” or “neglect”—to treat something as unworthy of proper attention or care. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 3:11, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. It describes an attitude or action of failing to value, heed, or attend to what should receive attention. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes something as “whole” or “entire,” emphasizing completeness rather than only a part. It can identify a person, object, or matter considered in its full extent, though the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:31. Its basic sense remains the idea of something complete, undivided, or taken as a whole.

Omousi, also rendered Omusi, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 6:19 and 1 Chronicles 6:4. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a broader meaning or word-concept beyond that personal designation.

Ouphir, also given as “Ufir,” is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a named figure in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Genesis 10:29. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name’s specific role there cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name “Ouphir” or “Ufir.”

This Greek Old Testament verb means “remove” or “put aside.” It describes taking something or someone out of a position, place, or situation. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel, so its normal sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the sentence and passage where it appears.

Pentapolis is a proper name for a place called “Pentapolis.” It identifies a particular location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX text represented here, it appears once, in Wisdom 10:6. The available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text, so it cannot explain the place’s specific role in that passage. Its basic meaning is therefore the name of the location itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “distract”: to draw someone’s attention or effort away from one matter toward another. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being diverted in the surrounding sentence. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, including three occurrences in Ecclesiastes. Its central idea remains the interruption or redirection of attention, concern, or activity.

This Greek LXX noun means “lock,” referring to a gathered or hanging portion of hair. It names the lock itself rather than describing an action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, at 3 Maccabees 1:4. Since the verse text is not included, the surrounding passage would be needed to explain exactly how this lock functions in that sentence. Its basic sense remains a lock of hair or a similar gathered strand.

This proper noun is a personal name, rendered “Posidōnios” or “Posithonios.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 14:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not available, the person’s specific role or significance cannot be stated from the name alone. The core meaning is therefore simply the individual’s name: Posidōnios, also known as Posithonios.

This noun means “choosing”—the act or result of selecting one option rather than another. It refers to a decision or chosen course, not merely to a passing thought. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 14 times, appearing especially in Ecclesiastes, with additional occurrences in Jeremiah and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being chosen and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “unite” or “approach.” It describes coming near or joining with someone or something, depending on the sentence. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is movement toward another or joining together. It is not a noun naming a person or thing, but an action word.

This word means “early”. It describes something that happens near the beginning of a day or before a later time. As an adjective, it can characterize a time, action, or event as early rather than late. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times, showing a consistent reference to an earlier time within different kinds of passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains simple: something belongs to the beginning or comes before what follows.

This noun means “citadel” or “fortress,” referring to a fortified place associated with protection and defense. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Psalm 121:7. Since it appears only once in this corpus, there are no other occurrences here for comparison. Its basic meaning is therefore clear as a word naming a fortified place, rather than an action, quality, or person. The precise force of the word in Psalm 121:7 depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Raemmath (also rendered Rhaemmath) is a proper name—the identifying name of a person or place in the Greek Old Testament text. Its lexical entry does not provide a broader descriptive meaning, so it should be understood as a name rather than translated as an ordinary quality, action, or object. It occurs exactly once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 11:14.

Reelias is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 2:2. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided here, the name itself does not supply further information about the person’s identity or role. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name Reelias, also rendered Rheelias in the lexical definition.

Sanaballat is a proper name referring to a person named Sanaballat, also rendered Sanavallat. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs ten times, all in Nehemiah. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is identifying the individual who bears it; the name itself does not express an action, quality, or general concept. The name appears from Nehemiah 2:10 through Nehemiah 13:28 in this Greek Old Testament corpus.

Saraias is a personal name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as “Saraias” or “Sareas.” It identifies people rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs eight times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, across passages in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Jeremiah. Because it is a name, its particular reference depends on the person identified in each passage; the name itself does not provide a broader abstract meaning.

Sedrach is a proper name, also rendered Sethrakh, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twelve times, chiefly in Daniel and once in Zechariah. The name is consistently represented as “Sedrach,” so its meaning here is its identity as a personal name. Understanding what Sedrach does or represents in any particular passage requires the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This Greek LXX noun means “wreath” or “laurel,” referring to a circular crown made from leaves or other material. Such a wreath could be placed on a person’s head as an adornment or honor. The word occurs 45 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so it is a recurring image rather than a rare term. Its exact force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and whether the wreath is being described as an object, an adornment, or a sign of distinction.

This verb means “gloomy”: it describes becoming dark, sorrowful, or troubled in appearance or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Ezekiel, so its recorded use is limited but consistent. The word points to a visibly or emotionally darkened condition rather than a specific action or object. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains gloom or deep distress.

This Greek LXX verb means “call together”: it describes summoning people so they assemble for a shared purpose. As a verb, it focuses on the act of bringing or gathering people together, rather than merely addressing one person. It occurs 10 times in the Greek LXX, across nine Old Testament occurrences and one Deuterocanonical occurrence. Its recorded uses span books such as Exodus, Joshua, Jeremiah, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees, showing a general word for convening people. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “confusion”: a state in which people or circumstances become mixed up, unsettled, or difficult to understand. It describes disorder rather than a person, object, or specific action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, including Genesis 11:9 and several passages in 1 Samuel. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a breakdown of clarity, order, or agreement.

This adjective means “short”: limited in length, duration, or extent. It describes something that is not long or prolonged, though the exact aspect being measured depends on the sentence around it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its basic meaning remains simple and concrete; the surrounding passage determines whether “short” concerns time, wording, distance, or another kind of extent.

Tanathan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Isaiah 20:1, and is rendered “Tanathan.” Because the available passage text is not included here, the person’s identity and role cannot be explained further from this word alone. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Tanathan within that single occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “cave” or “hole,” referring to an opening or hollow place in the ground or rock. It is a straightforward physical word rather than a title, action, or abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all in Isaiah, including passages that refer to people hiding in caves or holes. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene.

In the Greek Old Testament, this verb means “draw.” It describes the act of bringing something toward oneself or taking it out, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 12 times across 12 Old Testament verses, with several occurrences in Genesis 24. Its precise object and force depend on the sentence where it appears in its immediate context.

This noun means “pride”: an elevated, self-important attitude that places oneself above others or refuses proper submission. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures, it describes an inward posture rather than mere confidence or dignity. The word occurs 47 times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Psalms, Proverbs, and the deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use presents pride as an attitude recognized and condemned in scriptural instruction. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “remind”: to bring something back to a person’s attention or memory. It describes an action that causes someone to remember what they already knew, heard, or had been taught, rather than introducing an entirely new matter. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus—once in 1 Kings and three times in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “drug” or “medicine,” referring to a substance used for healing or other bodily purposes. Its basic sense is practical and material: it names a medicinal substance rather than a person, action, or character trait. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages from Exodus, Kings, Jeremiah, Daniel, Micah, Nahum, and Sirach. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a drug or medicine.

Phasour, also rendered Fasur, is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader action, quality, or concept; its normal function is to identify an individual. The name occurs twice in this corpus, once in Ezra 10:22 and once in Nehemiah 10:4. Without the surrounding verse text, the identity or role of the person cannot be explained further from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “pick the lice off.” It describes the act of removing lice, so it names a specific physical action rather than a general idea of cleansing or removing something. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah 50:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the deliberate picking off of lice.

This Greek LXX noun means “firewood”—wood gathered or used as fuel for a fire. It names a material rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Psalms 101:4, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its precise force in that verse belongs to the passage’s context, but the word itself refers plainly to wood intended for burning.

This word means “widow,” a woman whose husband has died. It is a noun naming her condition or social situation, and it is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books. The word occurs 66 times in this LXX corpus, including passages concerning widows in Genesis, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, and 1 Kings. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines what is said or required concerning the widow in that particular passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “of course meal,” referring to a meal or food made from course flour. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament tradition, at Genesis 40:16. Because the word is a noun and has no other recorded occurrences in this corpus, its meaning is narrowly focused rather than a broad description used in many settings. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly how this food is being mentioned there.

Ōbēth, also rendered Ovith, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person named in Ezra 8:6. Because it occurs only once in this corpus, its lexical record establishes the name but does not by itself explain the person’s role, family connection, or significance. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand how this individual fits into the account. It should therefore be read as a personal designation, not as a general term with an everyday definition.
